title: Does Implant Design Influence Bone Remodeling or Inflammation? A Prospective Study Comparing Tissue‑Level and Bone-Level Implants
content: (1) Background: Long-term dental implant performance depends on the interaction between mechanical load distribution and peri-implant tissue response. The influence of implant macro-design and vertical placement on early inflammatory signaling remains unclear. Therefore, the aim of this study is to compare tissue-level (TL) and bone-level (BL) implant configurations regarding marginal bone loss (MBL) and peri-implant inflammatory biomarkers. (2) Methods: In this prospective randomized trial, 23 healthy patients received 42 implants (21 TL, 21 BL). TL implants were placed at the crestal level, whereas BL implants were positioned 2 mm subcrestally and restored after 2 months using definitive transepithelial abutments (one-time abutment concept). MBL was assessed radiographically at prosthesis delivery, 1 year, and 2 years. Peri-implant crevicular fluid was collected at 1 year to determine IL-1β and MMP-8 levels by ELISA. (3) Results: At 2 years, mean MBL increase was significantly greater for TL than BL implants (0.55 vs. 0.29 mm; p < 0.05), with significant differences at medial (p = 0.0072) and distal (p = 0.0142) sites. BL remodeling remained within the protective 2-mm subcrestal bone. IL-1β and MMP-8 levels were higher in TL implants but without significant differences (p > 0.05). (4) Conclusions: Marginal bone remodeling appears to reflect physiological biomechanical adaptation rather than active inflammation. Subcrestal BL placement may provide a protective buffer against crestal bone loss without increasing local inflammatory activity.
